How should I answer comprehension questions to score high marks?

Follow this method every time.

Step 1: read the passage once quickly to get the general idea.
Step 2: read the QUESTIONS next, so you know what to look for.
Step 3: read the passage again slowly, underlining the parts that answer each question.
Step 4: answer in COMPLETE SENTENCES, in your own words where possible — copying whole chunks blindly rarely earns full marks.
Step 5: match your answer's length to the marks: one mark needs one point, three marks need three points.
Step 6: never bring in outside knowledge or opinions; every answer must come from the passage itself. Finally, watch the question word: 'state' wants a fact, 'explain' wants reasons, 'according to the passage' means the author's view, not yours. Leave no question blank — an attempted answer may earn something.

How do I work out the meaning of a word I don't know in a passage?

Use CONTEXT CLUES — the surrounding words that hint at the meaning. Four clue types to look for.

DEFINITION: the passage explains it directly, as in 'The drought, a long period without rain, destroyed the crops.'
CONTRAST: a word like but, although or unlike signals the opposite, as in 'Unlike his talkative brother, Musa was taciturn' — so taciturn means quiet.
EXAMPLE: 'Tubers such as yam, cassava and cocoyam grow underground' tells you what tubers are.
GENERAL SENSE: read the whole sentence and ask what word would fit, as in 'After trekking for hours under the hot sun, the farmer was famished and ate two plates of food' — famished must mean very hungry. Also break the word into parts: 'unhappy' is un- (not) plus happy. Guess from clues first, then confirm with a dictionary later.

What is a paragraph and how do I write a good one?

A paragraph is a group of sentences that develop ONE main idea. A good paragraph has three parts. The TOPIC SENTENCE states the main idea, usually first: 'Our school compound is very clean.' The SUPPORTING SENTENCES explain, give reasons or examples: 'Every morning, pupils sweep their assigned areas. The refuse bins are emptied daily, and flowers line the pathways.' The CONCLUDING SENTENCE rounds it off or links to the next idea: 'Visitors often praise how neat the environment looks.' Rules to follow: indent or leave a line at the start; keep to one idea per paragraph and start a new one when the idea changes; and aim for four to six sentences. A composition with no paragraphs is hard to read and loses organisation marks, no matter how good the content.

How do I write a good narrative composition?

A narrative tells a story, so it needs a clear structure.

INTRODUCTION: set the scene — who, where and when: 'It was the last day of the second term when our class went on an excursion to Olumo Rock.'
BODY: narrate events in the ORDER they happened, using time expressions like first, then, after that, suddenly and finally. Build towards the most exciting moment (the climax).
CONCLUSION: say how it ended and what you felt or learnt: 'We returned home tired but happy, and I will never forget that day.' Key tips: write mostly in the PAST tense and keep it consistent; use vivid details and the five senses; include a little direct speech to bring it alive; and stay strictly on the given topic. Plan for five minutes before writing — a jotted outline of your events prevents a rambling story.

What layout and parts does an informal letter need in a JSS1 exam?

An informal (friendly) letter goes to someone you know well — a friend or relative — and has five parts.

First, YOUR ADDRESS at the top right-hand corner, written line by line.
Second, the DATE directly under the address: '15th July, 2026.'
Third, the SALUTATION on the left: 'Dear Ada,' — always with a comma.
Fourth, the BODY in paragraphs: begin by asking after the person's wellbeing, then give your news or message, then close warmly.
Fifth, the SUBSCRIPT (closing): 'Your loving friend,' or 'Yours sincerely,' followed by your first name only.

Remember: an informal letter carries ONLY your own address, never the receiver's, and it has no heading or title. Keep the language warm and conversational — contractions like 'I'm' and 'don't' are perfectly acceptable here, unlike in a formal letter.

What is the difference between a formal and an informal letter?

They differ in audience, format and language.

AUDIENCE: an informal letter goes to friends and family; a formal letter goes to officials — your principal, an employer, a newspaper editor.
ADDRESSES: informal letters carry only your address; formal letters carry your address AND the receiver's address on the left.
HEADING: formal letters need a title stating the purpose, such as 'APPLICATION FOR A PLACE IN YOUR SCHOOL', usually underlined; informal letters have none.
SALUTATION AND CLOSING: informal uses 'Dear Chidi,' with 'Your loving friend,'; formal uses 'Dear Sir/Madam,' with 'Yours faithfully,' (or 'Yours sincerely,' when you know the name).
LANGUAGE: informal allows contractions and chatty expressions; formal requires full words, polite and serious tone, and no slang. Choosing the wrong register is a common and costly exam error.

How can I improve my vocabulary?

Vocabulary grows through deliberate daily habits.

First, READ widely — newspapers, storybooks and your textbooks — because reading exposes you to words in natural use.
Second, keep a VOCABULARY NOTEBOOK: write each new word, its meaning, and your OWN sentence using it; a word is only truly yours once you have used it.
Third, learn words in FAMILIES: from 'happy' you get happiness, unhappy, happily.
Fourth, study synonyms and antonyms so you can vary your writing instead of repeating 'good' and 'nice'.
Fifth, learn common prefixes and suffixes: un- and dis- mean not, re- means again, -ful means full of.
Sixth, USE new words when speaking and writing — five new words a week becomes over 250 a year.
Finally, always confirm meanings in a dictionary before using a word in an exam.

How do I find the main idea of a passage?

The main idea is what the whole passage is mostly about — not a small detail from one line. Use these steps.

Step 1: check the TITLE if there is one, as it often states the subject directly.
Step 2: read the FIRST and LAST paragraphs carefully; writers usually introduce the main idea early and restate it at the end.
Step 3: find the TOPIC SENTENCE of each paragraph and see what they have in common.
Step 4: ask yourself, 'If I had to tell a friend in one sentence what this passage is about, what would I say?' That sentence is the main idea.
Step 5: test your answer — the main idea must cover the WHOLE passage. If your statement only fits one paragraph, it is a supporting detail, not the main idea. Watch for repeated words, since writers repeat what matters most.
